SLOOS-adjusted summary:
- Policy stance: The FOMC kept the federal funds rate at 0–0.25% and continued monthly asset purchases ($80B Treasuries, $40B agency MBS) with strong forward guidance tied to achieving maximum employment and inflation moderately above 2% for some time.
- Macro backdrop: Activity and employment are strengthening amid vaccinations and policy support; inflation has risen but is described as largely transitory; outlook remains tied to the course of the virus.
- SLOOS lens on credit supply and demand:
  - Easing: Banks have eased standards across several categories, notably residential real estate (including GSE-eligible mortgages), HELOCs at large banks, and consumer credit (credit cards and auto), with some reductions in minimum credit score requirements. Standards for investment-grade C&I borrowers have eased at large banks; foreign banks report unchanged standards for IG borrowers.
  - Remaining tightness/divergence: Relative to pre-pandemic levels, standards are still tighter in many segments, and below-investment-grade C&I lending remains tight (foreign banks report tightening). Some large banks tightened certain C&I loan policies even as others eased.
  - Demand: C&I loan demand has been soft relative to pre-pandemic norms, while mortgage/household credit demand has been firmer.
- Net tone: SLOOS indicates improving credit availability that supports the FOMC’s accommodative stance and the recovery, but the improvement is uneven across borrower types and remains tighter than pre-pandemic for riskier credits. This nudges the overall tone modestly more positive than an FSR-driven view, but still measured given uneven credit conditions and lingering downside risks tied to the virus.
